demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
try hard not think about the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Several selected items imply a hypervigilance/physical-assault style threat profile (scanning exits, reacting to sudden movements, avoiding open spaces) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one. These items usually fit interpersonal violence, combat, or other danger-based trauma more than bereavement trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Rehearse Conversations before any interaction' suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding threat or memory items about social humiliation, blame, or feared conversations about the death. It sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile and does not clearly connect to the active Memory→Threat→Strategies formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: These items imply a danger-based, assault-like or combat-like threat profile centered on physical attack and environmental vulnerability, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat content is internally coherent with hypervigilance for interpersonal/physical danger, but that pattern is not clinically well matched to the rest of the profile, where memory items reflect disorganized recall of a death-related trauma rather than threat from current spaces, exits, or others' movements.

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard' is more typical of interpersonal violence/combat threat cues and is hard to reconcile with a trauma of unexpected death of a loved one when the rest of the profile centers on grief-related memory disturbance rather than current danger from people.

vignette:
Kofi is a 62-year-old stock broker, divorced, living alone in a high-rise apartment in downtown Chicago. He came to therapy at the urging of his adult daughter, who had grown alarmed by his increasing isolation and a recent incident at work that nearly cost him his license. The event that shattered his life happened three years ago, on a crisp October morning. His younger brother, Emmanuel, a healthy 58-year-old contractor, had come over for their weekly breakfast. Kofi was in the kitchen scrambling eggs when he heard a sharp gasp from the living room. He walked in to find Emmanuel slumped in the armchair, his face frozen in a grimace, one hand clutching his chest. Kofi called 911, performed chest compressions as the dispatcher instructed, but by the time the paramedres arrived, Emmanuel was gone. A massive coronary, the doctors said. No warning. No history. Just gone.

In the months that followed, Kofi found that he could not hold the full picture of that morning in his mind. When he tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events—what time Emmanuel arrived, what they had been talking about, the exact words the paramedic said—it felt like reaching for something in fog. The memory came only in sudden, jarring fragments: the sound of the gasp, the strange angle of his brother’s head against the chair, the cold slickness of the phone against his ear. These fragments would crash into him without warning. Once, while slicing an onion in his kitchen, he was suddenly back on the living room floor, his hands pumping against Emmanuel’s sternum, the smell of eggs burning somewhere. He dropped the knife and stood trembling for ten minutes.

Kofi began to interpret these intrusions as signs that he had failed. He went over and over it, replaying the morning in his head like a tape he could not stop: Why did I go to the kitchen? Why didn’t I check on him sooner? What if I had known CPR better? The questions circled endlessly, especially at night, and he came to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him, that he had missed a sign a good brother would have seen. The guilt was a constant companion, a hot, sharp shame that made him avoid his own reflection. He also felt a diffuse, frightening anger—at the doctors, at the paramedics who had been too slow, at Emmanuel for dying, and then at himself for being angry at a dead man.

To escape this, Kofi tried hard not to think about the trauma. He threw out the armchair. He stopped cooking eggs. He changed his route home to avoid the hospital where they had pronounced Emmanuel. But the most pervasive avoidance was of anything connected to his brother. He stopped answering calls from Emmanuel’s widow. He deleted old photos from his phone. He told his daughter not to mention Uncle Manny’s name. The consequence was a slow, painful contraction of his world. His other siblings grew frustrated and stopped inviting him to family gatherings. He had once been the family’s patriarch, the one who hosted Christmas; now he was the ghost who sent a check but never showed up.

At work, the emotional numbness and hyperarousal bled into his judgment. Kofi had always been a calculated risk-taker in the market, but now he found himself making reckless, impulsive trades—doubling down on volatile options, ignoring stop-losses, chasing losses with larger bets. It felt, he later admitted, like a way to make the internal noise stop, to feel something other than the crushing guilt. Last month, he lost a client $200,000 in a single afternoon. His firm put him on probation and strongly suggested he seek help. That was the moment his daughter drove him to the clinic.

What frightens Kofi most now is not the memory itself, but the belief that he is becoming a person he does not recognize—someone reckless, cold, and broken. He is terrified that if he lets himself really remember what happened, he will fall apart completely. But he is also, beneath that fear, quietly hoping that therapy might give him permission to grieve the brother he has been too afraid to mourn.
